meta.title: GPU Spend
meta.subtitle: Four months on one GPU cluster, in three questions. The workings, tables and caveats are in the report.
meta.caveat: MIT SuperCloud publishes this as a four-month sample of the cluster's jobs and says it is not appropriate for estimating system utilization. Figures describe the sample, not the cluster.

spine.name: Reserved, never used
spine.full_name: Held a GPU and never used it
spine.plain: The job reserved a GPU and never ran a single calculation on it, then failed, timed out or was cancelled.

now.note: These sit idle for days, not minutes. Hour-weighted, the typical one holds its GPU for 198 hours.

cut.action: End a job whose GPUs have sat at zero for an hour.
cut.owner: Platform team — a scheduler policy, no researcher action needed.

tradeoff.what_breaks: A job staging a large dataset, or running a long CPU preamble, that would have started computing after the grace period expired.
tradeoff.defence: A peak-guarded rule has no false positives in this data: a job at 0% average and 0% peak never ran a kernel. Lengthening the grace to 8 hours is the priced safety margin.

spine.name: Barely used
spine.plain: The job did compute at some point, but averaged under 5% of the card.

now.note: This is the bucket that looks cuttable and is not. Some of it is real work in short bursts.

cut.basis: Half of the idle share of these hours, because the other half is probably real work.
cut.action: Investigate the biggest owners before writing any rule.
cut.owner: Researchers who own the workflows, with platform support.

tradeoff.what_breaks: 2,564 jobs averaged under 5% but passed 50% at their busiest moment, and 45% of them completed. A rule keyed on average utilization kills them in the middle of real work.
tradeoff.defence: Key any rule on sustained zero, never on the average. Utilization is also a proxy: a job waiting on its data loader does real work at low occupancy.

spine.name: Didn't need a GPU
spine.full_name: Finished without ever using the GPU
spine.plain: The job completed successfully and never touched the GPU it was given. It is CPU work sitting in the GPU queue.

now.note: The strongest evidence in the data: the work succeeded without the card.

cut.basis: All of it. The job already proved it does not need a GPU.
cut.action: Default these workflows to CPU nodes.
cut.owner: Workflow owners — mostly a launcher default, not per-job.

tradeoff.what_breaks: 11,464 jobs crashed before reaching their GPU code. They look identical to this bucket but will need a card once the bug is fixed.
tradeoff.defence: Offload only jobs that completed without the GPU. Being wrong is cheap and visible: the job fails fast or runs slowly, and its owner resubmits with a GPU flag.

spine.name: Second GPU sat idle
spine.full_name: One card idle beside a working one
spine.plain: A multi-GPU job where one card worked and another sat unused for the whole run.

now.note: Invisible in the job table, which averages a job's cards. Only the per-card data shows it.

cut.basis: Half of the 14,558 idle card-hours. Right-sizing needs the owner to change code.
cut.action: Ask the owners to request one GPU instead of two.
cut.owner: Researchers — this is a code change, not a setting.

tradeoff.what_breaks: Nothing breaks if we are wrong, but nothing is recovered either. The saving only lands if the owner actually changes the request, and some code genuinely needs the second card later.
tradeoff.defence: Treat it as a conversation with a handful of owners rather than a policy. Half-counted here for that reason.

spine.name: Ran out of time
spine.full_name: Busy work destroyed at the time limit
spine.plain: The job was computing hard when its time limit expired and the scheduler killed it.

now.note: Real science, thrown away. It looks like waste in an outcome chart and is the opposite.

cut.basis: Nothing. This is not a cut.
cut.action: Checkpointing, so a rerun resumes instead of restarting.

tradeoff.what_breaks: Counting these hours as recoverable promises the CFO capacity that was already doing useful work. Cutting here does not free a GPU; it stops research.
tradeoff.defence: Report as lost work in a separate column from savings. The remedy saves reruns, not capacity.

spine.name: Used normally
spine.plain: Everything else: jobs that used the GPU they asked for.

now.note: The majority of the bill, and the part a 20% cut must not touch.

cut.basis: Nothing. This is the work the cluster exists for.

tradeoff.what_breaks: Any policy that reaches into this bucket is slowing research down, which is the one constraint the CFO was given.
tradeoff.defence: Every rule above is deliberately narrow so it cannot reach these hours.

tile1.reading: Read the buckets, not the outcomes. A cancelled job can be a researcher correctly killing a bad run, and a finished job can have barely touched its GPU. What the card was doing matters more than how the job ended.

tile2.title: Where to cut
tile2.question: How much of that comes back, and who has to do something?

kpis.sub: 24% of the bill, without slowing research down

low.basis: Half the CPU-work bucket, plus a 4-hour-grace idle kill. Nothing else counted.

point.basis: The per-bucket column on this tile, added up.

high.basis: No grace at all, and every idle and idle-card hour counted.

tile2.verdict: The point estimate clears a 20% cut. The cautious reading does not, and falls $95K short. Two thirds of the total is the near-certain part: GPUs that sat at zero for days.

grace_sweep.note: The idle kill barely depends on the grace period, because these jobs sit idle for days. Even a 24-hour grace returns most of the money.

tile3.title: What it costs if we're wrong
tile3.question: Each cut assumes something. What breaks if the assumption turns out to be false?

kpis.label: we are confident about
kpis.sub: these GPUs were switched on and never touched

kpis.label: depends on a judgment call
kpis.sub: low usage might still be real work

kpis.label: of real work we'd kill by mistake
kpis.sub: if we chased the bigger number and cut all low usage

risks.claim: Cut the GPUs that were never touched
risks.what_if_wrong: None of these 2,467 jobs ever ran a calculation, so there is nothing to lose. This is the part to promise.
Tempting, but it kills 2,099 jobs that finished successfully, including $101K of work that was busy in bursts and only looks idle on average.
No scheduler setting delivers this. Researchers have to change how their code asks for GPUs, so treat it as a target, not a saving.

risks.claim: Count jobs that ran out of time as waste
risks.what_if_wrong: These GPUs were working hard when the clock stopped them. The fix is longer limits or checkpointing, which costs money rather than saving it.

guards.label: Peak must be zero
guards.hint: Only jobs whose busiest moment was also 0%.

guards.label: Peak under 20%
guards.hint: Allows a brief spike, blocks sustained work.

simulator.note: A job at 0% average and 0% peak never ran a kernel, so a peak-guarded rule has no false positives inside this data. Everything above zero trades savings for damage.

definitions.question: Is a job its owner cancelled a waste of money?

options.label: Only the hours the card sat idle

definitions.why: Cancelled jobs ran at 34.3% hour-weighted utilization against the cluster's 38.5%. Cancelling is usually a researcher correctly killing a run that looked wrong — good practice, not waste. The idle time before the cancel is already counted in the buckets.

definitions.question: How much of the bill is recoverable?

options.label: Everything that did not become finished work

definitions.why: The first number is the brief's starting point and it is real. Promising it as a cut commits to recovering hours spent on work that finished, crashed for reasons a scheduler cannot fix, or was computing when it stopped.

definitions.question: What is the cluster's average utilization?
definitions.why: A third of the job records hold almost none of the compute, so counting jobs equally answers a different question from the one the CFO asked.

nodes.why: Ranking machines by failure count and by failure rate gives two different lists, because exposure runs from 4 to 1,114 jobs per machine. Before draining anything, check whether one researcher owns most of its failures.

limits.consequence: Utilization is one average and one peak per job. 'Idle the whole time' and 'idle on average' are indistinguishable unless the peak is also zero.

limits.limit: Utilization is a proxy for useful work
limits.consequence: A job bound on its data loader or on talking to other machines does real work at low occupancy. Low is a question, not a verdict.

limits.limit: Idle capacity is invisible where you would look for it
limits.consequence: Telemetry starts and stops with a job, so an unallocated GPU emits nothing. None of these figures describe time nobody booked.

limits.limit: This is a sample, not the whole cluster
limits.consequence: MIT publishes four months of jobs and says it is not appropriate for estimating system utilization. Every number describes this sample over this window.

tile3.reading: Same six buckets again. The column now shows what we are assuming, and what it costs to be wrong about it — which is why the cautious total in the previous section is the honest one to promise.
